Curiously, although the database contains reports of 144 deaths during robotic surgery, the circumstances involved were recorded in detail in only a tiny fraction of cases. However, over 60 percent of these incidents were caused by device malfunctions while the rest were caused by factors such as operator error and the inherent risks of the surgery.

So, we can say that at least 87 of the deaths were recorded as being due to device malfunction. The remaining are human error or because the surgery just didn't work.

87 out of 1,700,000 surgeries? That's 0.005%. I'd take those odds.

EDIT: Went back to the article and saw that the '144 deaths' is from thirteen years(2000 to 2013) of data and '1.7 million robotic procedures' is from six(2007 to 2013).

So the chance of a robot surgeon killing you is less than 0.005%.

EDIT2: Actually, since they don't give certain figures in the article, the only thing I can conclude is that there's no more than a 0.0085% chance. Probably less than 0.005% though.

EDIT3: Finally found an article about provider (operator) error in surgery. Most of what I could find was 'medical error' (possible drug does error etc)

The article takes data from 2002, of the 4658 surgeries considered there were 128 deaths, 38 of which were considered preventable errors. So that's about a 0.816% chance of being killed by your human surgeon.
